```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.align = "center")
library(knitr)
source(params$script)
OUT <- params$output
dir.create(OUT, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
show <- function(f) {
  p <- file.path(OUT, f)
  if (file.exists(p)) knitr::include_graphics(p) else invisible(NULL)
}
```

# What this document does

Two comparisons *inside* one catcheR run. They answer different questions and
should not be confused:

| | compares | answers |
|---|---|---|
| `compare_bc_libraries()` | the pooled **BC libraries** (`set1`, `set2` …), i.e. the barcode-to-gene CSVs | did each library come back, evenly, and with how many cells per construct |
| `compare_sublibraries()` | the sequencing **sublibraries** (`s1`, `s2` …), i.e. separate FASTQ pairs of the same cell pool | did the aliquots behave alike |

This is **not part of the catcheR package**: it is a standalone script plus
this document, so it can be adapted per experiment without touching the
package. It reads the `.rds` the entry point already wrote — nothing is
re-streamed and it knits in seconds. Run the chemistry's own template first.

To point it at another run, change the parameters in the header:

```r
rmarkdown::render("catcheR_library_comparison.Rmd", params = list(
  run_object   = "analysis_EB_PIP/Output/pipcatch_AB019b.rds",
  called_cells = "analysis_EB_PIP/scratch/AB019b_gex.scRNA.filtered.barcodes.tsv.gz",
  tag          = "pipseq_AB019b"))
```

```{r load}
stopifnot(file.exists(params$run_object))
res <- readRDS(params$run_object)
cal <- if (nzchar(params$called_cells) && file.exists(params$called_cells))
         params$called_cells else NULL
kable(data.frame(
  object        = basename(params$run_object),
  chemistry     = class(res)[1],
  BC_libraries  = length(unique(res$reference_table$set)),
  sublibraries  = nrow(res$per_sublibrary),
  called_cells  = if (is.null(cal)) "not supplied" else basename(cal)))
```

The called-cell list matters as much here as anywhere: without it the counts
include the ambient floor, which is not evidence about either library.

# The pooled BC libraries

Each library is scored against **its own size**, taken from the run's reference
table, so a 60-construct library is never scored out of 100.

```{r libraries}
L <- compare_bc_libraries(res, called = cal, output_dir = OUT,
                          file = paste0(params$tag, "_bc_libraries"), verbose = FALSE)
kable(L[, c("library", "constructs_expected", "constructs_detected", "dropout",
            "pct_detected", "cells", "cells_per_construct", "clones")],
      caption = "Recovery and yield per BC library")
kable(L[, c("library", "cv_cells", "top_decile_share", "gini_cells", "median_cells")],
      caption = "Evenness within each library")
```

```{r lib-fig, fig.cap="The pooled BC libraries, compared"}
show(paste0(params$tag, "_bc_libraries.png"))
```

Three things to read, in order:

1. **Dropout** (panel A) — constructs in the reference that were never the
   dominant call in any cell. A library with systematically more dropout than
   its partner was under-represented in the pool or lost in cloning, and that
   is worth knowing before any biology is interpreted.
2. **Evenness** (panel B) — a library can detect every construct and still be
   unusable if a tenth of them hold most of the cells. The ranked curve shows
   the skew; CV, top-decile share and Gini quantify it.
3. **Yield per construct** (panel C) — the fair comparison between pools of
   different size.

```{r cross}
kable(data.frame(cells_with_calls_from_more_than_one_library = attr(L, "cross_set_cells")),
      caption = "Candidate doublets")
```

Cells carrying calls from more than one library are counted once, under the
library of their dominant clone, and reported separately: they are candidate
doublets, not evidence about either library.

One trap the script handles and a quick hand-rolled table usually does not: the
control constructs — `SCR1`, `SCR2`, `LUCIFERASE`, `B2M`, `ARHGDIA` — carry the
**same shRNA name in both libraries** (10 of the 160 names on this reference).
Keying on the name alone credits one detection to both and inflates every
per-library count, so the script keys on `(shRNA, set)` and uses the library
the cell's dominant call actually came from.

```{r per-construct}
pc <- attr(L, "per_construct")
kable(head(pc[order(pc$set, -pc$cells), ], 10),
      caption = "Per construct, ranked (full table in the CSV; dropouts are rows of zero)")
```

# The sequencing sublibraries

```{r sublibraries}
S <- try(compare_sublibraries(res, called = cal, output_dir = OUT,
                              file = paste0(params$tag, "_sublibraries"), verbose = FALSE),
         silent = TRUE)
if (inherits(S, "try-error")) {
  cat("Skipped:", conditionMessage(attr(S, "condition")))
} else {
  kable(S[, c("sublibrary", "read_pairs", "pct_cassette", "cells", "pct_one_clone",
              "median_depth", "constructs", "clones", "pct_clones_shared")],
        caption = "Per sequencing aliquot")
}
```

```{r sub-fig, fig.cap="The sequencing sublibraries, compared"}
show(paste0(params$tag, "_sublibraries.png"))
```

Aliquots of one cell pool are **expected** to share clones — a clone is a
population of cells, and its members distribute across aliquots — so a high
`pct_clones_shared` is normal and is reported rather than flagged. The reading
that would deserve attention is the opposite: near-zero sharing between
aliquots that should contain the same cells.

Panel B is the one most likely to show a real asymmetry, since it reflects how
hard each aliquot was sequenced rather than anything about the biology.

A run with a single FASTQ pair has nothing to compare on this axis, and the
chunk above says so instead of drawing a one-bar chart.
